note: Common beliefs about drugs and overdose that are wrong, each with the source that says so. Rules for editing: state the belief as people actually say it, keep the correction to a sentence or two, and never add an entry without a source that supports the specific claim being corrected. An uncited debunk is just a competing assertion, and this is the one page where the reader arrives believing the opposite.
intro: Things people are told that are not true. Every correction below is sourced — follow the links if any of it contradicts what you have heard.

items.myth: Put them in a cold shower to bring them round.
items.truth: It raises the risk of falling, drowning and shock. SAMHSA lists it as a don't.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: You have naloxone, so rescue breathing is not needed.
items.truth: Rescue breathing can be lifesaving on its own, and naloxone takes minutes to work.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: Slap them hard or shake them awake.
items.truth: Forceful stimulation only causes injury. Shout, then rub your knuckles on their sternum; if that fails they are unconscious.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: Inject them with saltwater, milk or a stimulant.
items.truth: None of it works. The only appropriate treatment is an opioid overdose reversal medication.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: Make them throw up whatever they swallowed.
items.truth: Choking or inhaling vomit can cause a fatal injury.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: They are breathing again, so it is over.
items.truth: Most opioids outlast the naloxone. Stay at least four hours from the last dose.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: They are just asleep — let them sleep it off.
items.truth: Deep sedation looks like sleep and is not. Put them on their side and stay.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: They can hear you, so they are fine.
items.truth: A high enough dose of ketamine leaves someone awake, aware and unable to respond or call for help.

sources.name: Poison Control — What is pink cocaine?

items.myth: You can overdose by touching fentanyl.
items.truth: Incidental skin contact is unlikely to cause toxicity, and no responder has been reported with opioid toxicity from it. Soap and water removes it.

sources.name: ACMT and AACT position statement — occupational fentanyl exposure
Same statement, PubMed

items.myth: Fentanyl in the air will drop you just from being in the room.
items.truth: Street fentanyl is not volatile. Where particles are actually airborne, an N95 is enough.

sources.name: ACMT and AACT position statement — occupational fentanyl exposure
Same statement, PubMed

items.myth: You need a hazmat suit to be near it.
items.truth: Nitrile gloves are sufficient for routine handling.

sources.name: ACMT and AACT position statement — occupational fentanyl exposure
Same statement, PubMed

items.myth: Giving naloxone to someone who has not taken opioids will hurt them.
items.truth: In another emergency it generally has no effect and causes no additional harm.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)

items.myth: Having naloxone around makes people use more.
items.truth: A systematic review of seven studies and 2,578 people found no evidence of it.

sources.name: Systematic review of a naloxone 'moral hazard' (Int J Drug Policy, 2021)

items.myth: There is xylazine in it, so naloxone is pointless.
items.truth: Naloxone does nothing to xylazine, but xylazine is nearly always mixed with fentanyl. Give it.

sources.name: CDC — What you should know about xylazine

items.myth: Medetomidine means naloxone will not work.
items.truth: It works on the fentanyl it is mixed with. Check breathing before you check whether they respond.

sources.name: PA Department of Health HAN #794 (relaying Philadelphia DPH)

items.myth: Nitazenes need many times the usual amount of naloxone.
items.truth: The published evidence does not support that.

sources.name: Comparative review, 2025
CDC MMWR — nitazenes

items.myth: A reagent kit will find fentanyl.
items.truth: Reagents react to whatever there is most of. Fentanyl is active far below what a color change can show.

sources.name: Two brands of fentanyl test strips against 251 synthetic opioids (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

items.myth: Pure fentanyl reacts, so a reagent would catch it.
items.truth: Consumer fentanyl averaged 10% by weight in Los Angeles drug checking. What reacts is the filler.

sources.name: Fentanyl purity in consumer samples, Los Angeles 2023–25 (preprint)

items.myth: One line on a test strip means it is clean.
items.truth: It is the other way round. One line is positive; the drug being there makes a line disappear.

sources.name: Two brands of fentanyl test strips against 251 synthetic opioids (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

items.myth: A faint second line is a positive.
items.truth: Any second line, however faint, is negative. Wait the full time — a faint line can appear and then fade.

sources.name: Two brands of fentanyl test strips against 251 synthetic opioids (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

items.myth: A negative strip clears the whole bag.
items.truth: It speaks for the pinch you dissolved. Fentanyl is not spread evenly.

sources.name: Two brands of fentanyl test strips against 251 synthetic opioids (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

items.myth: Test strips just give people false confidence.
items.truth: A positive result is associated with using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone close.

sources.name: Test strip results and change in drug use behavior (Int J Drug Policy, 2025)
Drug use behaviors among people who do and do not use test strips (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

items.myth: Xylazine strips catch xylazine.
items.truth: In one Los Angeles study of 333 fentanyl-positive samples they missed a large share.

sources.name: Test strip field performance, Los Angeles

items.myth: Nitazene strips catch nitazenes.
items.truth: A lab evaluation found 24 of 33, and they need a fairly large amount to be present.

sources.name: Nitazene test strip evaluation, 2024

items.myth: A reagent can tell you what a pink powder is.
items.truth: It reads the majority. A powder that is 80% ketamine reads as ketamine, whatever else is in it.

sources.name: DEA — Pink cocaine

items.myth: Test strips are illegal.
items.truth: Legal in most states, not all. As of July 2026 the ones where drug-checking equipment may still be criminal are Iowa, North Dakota and Texas — and the five-state lists circulating online are out of date.

sources.name: LAPPA — Drug Checking Equipment 50-State Summary (Sept 2025)

items.myth: Nitazenes are hundreds of times stronger than fentanyl.
items.truth: True of some members in lab tests, not of the family. Some are weaker than fentanyl.

sources.name: CDC MMWR — nitazenes
Comparative review, 2025

items.myth: Xylazine wounds are a flesh-eating infection.
items.truth: They are not. The leading explanation is blood vessels constricting and tissue being starved of blood.

sources.name: Philadelphia DPH — xylazine wound care

items.myth: Medetomidine causes wounds like xylazine does.
items.truth: Health officials state it does not appear to.

sources.name: PA Department of Health HAN #794 (relaying Philadelphia DPH)

items.myth: You can tell by looking, or by taste.
items.truth: Counterfeit pills are pressed to match, and fentanyl is active in amounts too small to see or taste.

sources.name: Fentanyl purity in consumer samples, Los Angeles 2023–25 (preprint)

items.myth: They woke up angry, so they are ungrateful.
items.truth: Waking into precipitated withdrawal is documented and studied. It is not about you.

sources.name: Neale et al., J Substance Abuse Treatment (2020)

items.myth: Your tolerance is where you left it.
items.truth: It drops after any break — jail, hospital, treatment, illness — and a previously normal amount can cause an accident.

sources.name: SAMHSA Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit (2023)
